query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Cold rolling followed by optimized low-temperature annealing of the eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy will refine the grain structure and induce the formation of fine B2 precipitates, thereby enhancing strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance under harsh service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with suboptimal strength and plasticity for industrial fastener applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical processing route consisting of cold rolling with a significant reduction followed by controlled low-temperature annealing designed to promote ultrafine grain refinement and B2 precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: The processed alloy should be tested under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to salt solutions) typical of fastener applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grains produced via cold working and controlled recovery/recrystallization, together with a uniform dispersion of fine B2 precipitates along grain boundaries and deformation structures.
generation.mechanism: The refinement of the grain structure enhances yield strength through the Hall-Petch effect, while the B2 precipitates contribute dispersion strengthening and hinder dislocation motion, thereby improving resistance to creep and mitigating corrosion-induced degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting alloy, the intervention is expected to yield a material with significantly improved yield strength and tensile strength, enhanced plasticity, better creep resistance at room temperature, and improved corrosion resistance under cyclic temperature and corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the as-cast uniform fine lamellar alloy currently exhibit insufficient strength and ductility for extreme service conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected when annealing temperatures are optimized to avoid excessive recrystallization or grain coarsening, and the processing is performed within parameters that mimic industrial-scale fastener service conditions. The operating window includes low-temperature annealing below the temperature at which abnormal grain growth or unwanted phase transformations occur.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvements (increased strength and ductility alongside better creep and corrosion resistance) are expected based on analogous HEA systems, the precise quantitative gains and the long-term stability of the ultrafine grains and B2 precipitates under cyclic extreme conditions require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, subjecting them to identical cold rolling reductions, then anneal at a series of low temperatures (e.g., 800°C, 850°C, 900°C) for optimized durations. Use a control group of as-cast lamellar state specimens. Characterize the resultant microstructures with TEM/SEM to confirm ultrafine grain sizes and verify the formation of fine B2 precipitates. Subsequently, conduct tensile tests, creep experiments at room temperature, and corrosion testing (e.g., salt spray or cyclic immersion) under conditions replicating fastener service environments.
measurements: Volume fraction and size of B2 precipitates via image analysis.
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility via standardized mechanical tests.
Creep strain rate at room temperature.
Corrosion rate and pitting resistance in accelerated corrosion tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (strength, ductility, and creep resistance) and enhanced corrosion resistance relative to the unprocessed baseline, or if the intended microstructural changes (ultrafine grains and B2 precipitates) are not reproducibly achieved, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The room-temperature strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is relatively low owing to its intrinsic fcc structure. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. It was found that the large and spherical B2 precipitates were generated in the recrystallized grain boundaries of three annealing states, while the small and elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealing state. The former B2 precipitates assisted in refining the recrystallized grains to quasi ultra-fine grain and fine grain regimes (with the grain sizes of ~0.9, ~2.2, and ~7.2 μm). The tensile results indicated that the decreased annealing temperature induced the gradual strengthening of this alloy but also maintained the ductility at the high levels. reading.lever: Apply cold rolling followed by optimized low-temperature annealing to induce ultrafine grain refinement and B2 precipitate formation.
reading.why: This approach, validated in a related Al-containing HEA system, directly targets the balance of strength and ductility needed under extreme mechanical and corrosive conditions.
